summary: Presents the Softwire Mesh framework for carrying IPv4 and IPv6 across single-protocol networks, such as ones that handle only IPv4 or only IPv6. The goal is for both to work on the Internet as the transition takes place.

plainLanguage.summary:
Some networks in the Internet handle only one version of IP. This RFC explains how such a network can still carry the other version across, by passing the routing information around the edge and tunnelling the data through the middle.

The framework leaves the choice of tunnelling technology to the operator, and says how the routing information has to be shaped so that the two versions fit together.

questions: how to carry ipv6 over an ipv4 only core
how to carry ipv4 over an ipv6 only core
what is the softwire mesh framework
how does a softwire carry ipv6 over ipv4
subtitle: How a network built for one version of IP can carry the other version across.

tldr.problem: Some networks in the Internet can only handle one version of IP, but they still have to carry the other version for the clients attached to them.
tldr.mechanism: The edge routers exchange the client protocol's routes over BGP on the core protocol, then wrap each packet in an encapsulation header the core routers understand and tunnel it across. Those tunnels are called softwires.
tldr.outcome: A single-protocol backbone can provide transit for the other protocol without changing its interior routers. The framework picks no tunnelling technology and leaves that to policy, and points at other documents for the signalling.

facts.label: Tunnelling technologies accommodated
facts.value: MPLS (LDP and RSVP-TE), L2TPv3, GRE, IP-in-IP

facts.label: Routers that must support both families

today: RFC 5565 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It is a framework document, so it defines no message format of its own: the BGP-based signalling it calls for is specified in RFC 5512, and the IPsec tunnel attributes in RFC 5566.

sections.title: The Single-Protocol Core Problem
sections.content:
The Internet has to carry both IPv4 and IPv6 packets, but parts of it are expected to be single-protocol networks. One kind can parse only IPv4 packets and holds only IPv4 routing information; another kind can parse only IPv6 packets and holds only IPv6 routing information. Either kind still has to provide transit service for the other protocol.

The document explains how: the routing information of the other protocol is passed from one edge of the single-protocol network to the other, and the data packets of the other protocol are tunnelled across. Those tunnels are called softwires. The framework is careful to say when the job can be done with existing technology and when it needs new or modified technology.

The framework builds on the notion of a backbone whose interior routers do not keep external routing information. Traditionally BGP distributes external routes to every router in the backbone, and each interior router looks at each packet header to find the matching route. That is native forwarding. With tunneled forwarding the edge router adds an encapsulation header, so the interior routers read only the encapsulation header and send the packet to the right edge router, which removes the header at the far end. The scenario is sometimes called a BGP-free core, which the RFC calls a misnomer, since the point is not that interior routers do not run BGP but that they do not maintain the external routing information.
sections.plainLanguage: Some networks in the Internet handle only one version of IP. This RFC explains how such a network can still carry the other version across, by passing the routing information around the edge and tunnelling the data through the middle.

sections.title: Two Scenarios and Three Router Roles
sections.content:
The framework covers two scenarios that mirror each other. In the IPv6-over-IPv4 scenario the client networks run IPv6 and the backbone runs IPv4. In the IPv4-over-IPv6 scenario the client networks run IPv4 and the backbone runs IPv6. The RFC notes that IPv6-over-IPv4 has received a lot of attention while IPv4-over-IPv6 has not, even though service providers building IPv6 backbones still have large IPv4 networks and applications to carry across them. Neither scenario assumes that the only path between two client networks runs through the transit core, so the routing solution has to work in any topology.

Three kinds of router are involved. Customer Edge (CE) routers sit outside the backbone and are directly attached to it. Provider Edge (PE) routers are the edge of the backbone, with the ingress PE where a packet enters and the egress PE where it leaves. Interior routers are often called P routers. In this framework the edge routers are called Address Family Border Routers (AFBRs), because they are the ones that support both address families. The CE routers support only the client protocol and the P routers support only the core protocol.

The document gives the two address families short names: I-IP is the form of IP that the transit network supports, and E-IP is the form the client networks support. In the scenarios of interest E-IP is IPv4 if and only if I-IP is IPv6, and E-IP is IPv6 if and only if I-IP is IPv4.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework describes two mirrored cases: client networks on IPv6 over an IPv4 backbone, and client networks on IPv4 over an IPv6 backbone. The routers at the edge of the backbone handle both versions; the routers in the middle handle only one.

sections.title: Routing and Tunneled Forwarding
sections.content:
The P routers and the AFBRs take part in an interior gateway protocol, such as OSPF or IS-IS, to distribute I-IP routing information. The AFBRs use internal BGP to exchange E-IP routing information with each other, either in a full mesh or through a route reflector. The route information that travels is E-IP, but the BGP sessions themselves run over I-IP, and the BGP next hop of each E-IP route is an I-IP address.

When an ingress AFBR receives an E-IP packet on a client-facing interface it looks up the destination address. The best match will be a BGP route whose next hop is the I-IP address of another AFBR, the egress AFBR. The ingress AFBR forwards the packet through a softwire, by adding an encapsulation header that the P routers can process and that will carry the packet to the egress AFBR. The egress AFBR extracts the payload, which is the original E-IP packet, and forwards it on by looking up its IP destination address.

Adding an encapsulation header always makes the packet longer, so the maximum transmission unit of the softwire path SHOULD be large enough that no packet needs to be fragmented before it is encapsulated and no encapsulated packet needs to be fragmented on the way.
sections.plainLanguage: Edge routers exchange the routes for the client protocol over BGP, even though the BGP sessions run on the core protocol. When an edge router has a packet for a client network, it wraps the packet in a header the core routers understand and sends it to the far edge router, which takes the wrapper off.

sections.title: Advertising Routes with a Next Hop in the Other Family
sections.content:
Because the BGP updates travel over sessions that use the core protocol and are not tunnelled, a route for an E-IP prefix has to carry a next hop in the I-IP family. If a BGP speaker advertises itself as the next hop for such a route, it MUST, unless policy overrides it, specify the next hop address in the I-IP family. The address family of the next hop MUST NOT be changed by a route reflector.

Each pair of address families has its own procedure for encoding the next hop. For an IPv6 route with an IPv4 next hop, RFC 4798 explains the encoding; for an IPv4 route with an IPv6 next hop, RFC 5549 explains it. Where such a procedure depends on a BGP capability, all the AFBRs in a given transit core MUST advertise that capability.

Which of an AFBR's own addresses it uses in the next hop field is normally up to the administrator, with one exception. If the AFBR expects to receive packets through a softwire of a particular technology, and that technology knows the AFBR by a specific address, then that same address must be used in the BGP next hop field. With L2TPv3, for example, the address used for L2TPv3 signalling has to be the address used in the next hop field.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the routing messages travel over the core protocol, the address of the next hop must be in the core protocol's address family, even when the route itself belongs to the client protocol. The RFC also insists that an edge router is reachable at the same address by both routes and tunnels.

sections.title: Setting Up the Softwires
sections.content:
Before packets can flow, the softwires must be in place. With N dual-stack AFBRs, a mesh of point-to-point tunnels would need N^2 tunnels, so manual configuration of point-to-point tunnels is not part of this framework. Since the core provides a layer 3 transit service, multipoint-to-point tunnels are enough: in such a tunnel there is no way to tell which router put a packet into it, which matches the native IP model in which the egress router cannot tell the ingress router either. Point-to-point tunnels are allowed, for instance where quality of service or security needs them, but they are not required.

Where the tunnelling technology has its own signalling, that signalling is used. That covers MPLS softwires with LDP or RSVP-TE, and IPsec softwires with IKEv2 and IPsec. GRE has no native signalling, and the native L2TPv3 signalling sets up point-to-point tunnels, so the BGP-based signalling described in RFC 5512 covers the softwire cases for both. IP-in-IP, and GRE without optional header fields, need no signalling at all, because the only information the ingress AFBR needs is the egress address, which BGP already distributes.

Some fields of the encapsulation header are decided by policy at the ingress AFBR rather than by signalling or by routing, such as the time to live and the Diffserv bits. The RFC also asks that the softwires be always on, set up at system startup or triggered by the arrival of BGP routing information, so that no packet arrives before the tunnel it needs exists.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnels have to exist before the packets do. The framework avoids asking an operator to build a full mesh of point-to-point tunnels, which would grow with the square of the number of edge routers. Signalling comes from the tunnelling technology itself where there is one, and from BGP where there is not.

sections.title: Choosing a Tunnel and a Softwire for a Packet
sections.content:
Whether a packet goes through a softwire instead of being forwarded natively is decided by policy at the ingress AFBR. Simple policies include: send a packet through a softwire when routing says it must leave on a core-facing interface, when the interface it must leave on carries only I-IP packets, when the BGP next hop is an I-IP address, or whenever the best match is a BGP route, which tunnels all BGP-routed packets.

Which tunnelling technology to use is also policy, and is expected to be the same at all the AFBRs of a core, such as always L2TPv3 or always LDP-based MPLS. Mixed fleets can be handled by giving the administrators a small set of classes, making each AFBR a member of one or more of them, and advertising those memberships. RFC 5512 gives a way to do that, with BGP communities or extended communities in many cases, so that a policy can read as use L2TPv3 to talk to routers in class X and use GRE to talk to routers in class Y. Policies may also depend on the traffic class, on quality of service, or on characteristics of individual prefixes, and the RFC leaves such policies out of scope.

Once a packet is to go through a softwire, the BGP next hop address in the core address family is the address of the softwire's remote endpoint, and the packet MUST be sent through a softwire whose remote endpoint address is the same as that next hop. The encapsulation header needs nothing more for LDP-based MPLS, IP-in-IP or plain GRE. L2TPv3 and GRE with optional header fields need extra information from the remote endpoint, which RFC 5512 describes. RSVP-TE-based MPLS and IPsec use the native signalling of those technologies.
sections.plainLanguage: Two choices are left to the operator: whether a packet is tunnelled at all, and which tunnelling technology carries it. Both are set as policy at the edge router. The second choice can depend on what the far-end router supports, which the edge routers advertise to each other.

sections.title: Maintenance, Management and Multicast
sections.content:
Softwires are tunnels between routers, so they can break or slow down. The RFC lists ways to watch the status of the tunnel endpoints and of the tunnels themselves, which allow softwire path tracing, pinging a remote softwire endpoint and detecting that a remote endpoint has stopped being reachable. The examples given are BGP or TCP timeouts between AFBRs, ICMP or label switched path echo requests addressed to a particular AFBR, and Bidirectional Forwarding Detection packet exchanges between AFBRs. Another option is a softwire echo request sent to a well-known UDP port, carrying the egress AFBR address and the softwire identifier as the payload, encapsulated and forwarded in band along the same path as the softwire itself. Such a mechanism can be run periodically to check reachability, trading the cost of the check against how quickly a loss of reachability is noticed. The RFC says a framework for softwire operations and maintenance can largely be based on RFC 4176.

On management, MIBs exist for parts of the framework and will need to be extended or added to cover the functional elements that can be managed in the softwire network.

On multicast, the RFC supports PIM-SM and PIM-SSM across the core, and does not provide for BIDIR-PIM, BSR or AutoRP because these are not typically used across inter-provider boundaries. Two families of scheme are described. In a one-to-one mapping, each client multicast tree is extended through the core as exactly one tree; with PIM in the core, the AFBR translates the PIM control message from E-IP to I-IP and adds an RPF Vector naming the egress AFBR, because the core routers have no routes to E-IP addresses. With mLDP and multicast MPLS in the core, client SSM trees are mapped one to one onto point-to-multipoint label switched paths, with the (S,G) pair encoded into the FEC identifier. The second family treats all the AFBRs of a core as if they were PE routers attached to the same multicast VPN, which does not need a one-to-one mapping but does require the number of trees in the core to scale less than linearly with the number of client trees.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework says how to check that the tunnels are alive, using timeouts, echo requests or link probes. It also covers running multicast across the core, and it limits itself to the two multicast modes that are normally used between separate providers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The payload packets carried inside a softwire are ordinary E-IP packets travelling through the Internet, and the fact that they are inside a softwire does not change their security needs. The only security issues the RFC treats are those affecting the I-IP encapsulation headers, because those headers decide where the packets go and must appear in the clear.

Each receiving endpoint of a tunnel has one or more valid transmitting endpoints, those authorised to send it tunnelled packets. If the encapsulation header has no guarantee of authentication or integrity, unauthorised nodes can spoof tunnelled packets so that they look as if they came from an authorised endpoint, and they can replay packets. The damage is limited, because the receiving endpoint decapsulates the payload and routes it by the destination address inside the payload, and that address comes from the globally unique address space. A spoofed packet therefore cannot be delivered anywhere else. What an attacker can do is bypass policy at the authorised endpoint, and mount a denial of service, which cryptographic checks cannot prevent, because doing the cryptography on spoofed packets only makes the flooding worse.

Where a tunnel lies inside one administrative domain, non-cryptographic techniques are available. The receiving endpoints can be given their own addresses, and border routers can drop packets for those addresses that arrive from outside the domain. The transmitting endpoints can likewise be given their own addresses, so border routers drop outside packets with those source addresses and receiving endpoints discard softwire packets from anywhere else. With an MPLS encapsulation, border routers can refuse MPLS packets from outside the domain, or refuse those whose top label matches a tunnel endpoint. A cleartext password in the encapsulation header, such as the 64-bit L2TPv3 cookie, is another option inside a domain, since an arbitrary 64-bit value cannot be brute forced, but it is equally inapplicable to tunnels that cross domain boundaries.

Where the path between the endpoints is not secure enough, the RFC requires that a control protocol used to set up the tunnels have an authentication mechanism, and says that the MD5-based authentication of BGP is satisfactory when the tunnels are set up from BGP information. Data transmission should be secured with IPsec, used with an IP-based tunnelling mechanism. IPsec MUST provide authentication and integrity, so an implementation MUST support either ESP with null encryption or AH; ESP with encryption MAY be supported. Because the softwires are set up automatically as a side effect of routing information, key distribution MUST be automatic, by IKEv2, and the IPsec Tunnel Authenticator sub-TLV of RFC 5566 MUST be used and validated if no public key infrastructure is available.
sections.plainLanguage: The data inside the tunnel needs the same protection it would get anywhere else. The new risk is the outer header, because a forged one could make a packet look as if it came from an approved edge router, or could flood a tunnel endpoint. Border routers can filter for that inside one operator's network, and IPsec is the answer between networks.

layers.label: AFBR
layers.detail: Encapsulates the packet and sends it into the softwire

layers.label: Transit core
layers.detail: Runs the internal protocol, I-IP, and never looks inside the packet

layers.label: AFBR
layers.detail: Removes the encapsulation and forwards the original packet

viz.caption: ILLUSTRATIVE: ONE PACKET CROSSING A SOFTWIRE

messages.label: E-IP packet
messages.note: The original packet, sent to the client-facing interface.

messages.label: Encapsulated packet
messages.note: The packet with an encapsulation header addressed to the egress AFBR.

messages.label: Same encapsulated packet
messages.note: The core routers read only the encapsulation header.

messages.label: E-IP packet
messages.note: The encapsulation is removed and the original packet is forwarded on.

items.title: MPLS
items.text: Signalled with LDP or RSVP-TE. Optional at the edge routers and in the core.

items.title: L2TPv3
items.text: Native signalling builds point-to-point tunnels, so softwires need the BGP-based signalling of RFC 5512.

items.title: GRE
items.text: No native signalling. Plain GRE needs none; GRE with optional fields needs RFC 5512.

items.title: IP-in-IP
items.text: Needs no signalling, since only the egress address is required.

items.title: IPsec
items.text: Used when security requirements demand it, with IKEv2 for key distribution.
